ch11.anchor: life and death are decreed by fate
ch11.note: An echo of the Analects: 'Life and death are decreed by fate; wealth and honor rest with Heaven' (死生有命，富贵在天)—a saying of Confucius's disciple Zixia, invoked as fatalistic comfort in the face of danger.

Butterfield & Swire (太古) and Jardine, Matheson & Co. (怡和) were the two great British trading and shipping houses—'hongs'—that dominated commerce along the China coast from the treaty-port era; their steamers ran the Tianjin–Shanghai and Yangtze routes.

'Annam' was the older, French-colonial name for Vietnam (strictly its central region); 'Annamese,' used throughout these Hanoi chapters, means the Vietnamese people and their language. Hanoi was then the capital of French-ruled Tonkin in northern Vietnam.

The Comintern (Communist International, 1919–43) was the Moscow-directed body coordinating the world's Communist parties. The Anti-Comintern Pact, signed by Germany and Japan in 1936 and joined by Italy in 1937, aligned them ostensibly against it; 'joint defense against communism' was the banner under which Wang Jingwei justified his accommodation with Japan.

Imai Takeo (今井武夫, 1898–1982), a Japanese army officer who ran the General Staff's China section and was a principal in the covert negotiations that drew Wang Jingwei out of Chongqing; he worked alongside Kagesa Sadaaki on the Japanese side of the affair.

The South Manchuria Railway (南満洲鉄道, 'Mantetsu'), a huge Japanese semi-governmental corporation founded in 1906. Far more than a railway, it ran mines, harbors, and industry across Manchuria and maintained a famous research and intelligence arm—so a 'Mantetsu man' was often an agent of Japanese expansion.
Japanese shokutaku (嘱託), a specially commissioned contract employee or adviser attached to an office outside its regular staff—a convenient status for someone doing quiet or deniable work.

The private legal secretaries who drafted documents and briefs for imperial officials were proverbially men of Shaoxing in Zhejiang, famed—and feared—for their sly mastery of words. 'A Shaoxing clerk's brush' is thus a byword for cunning, sophistical pettifogging.

Chen Bulei (陈布雷, 1890–1948), Chiang Kai-shek's trusted confidential secretary and chief drafter of his speeches and statements—often called 'Chiang's brush.' His memoirs, quoted here, carried the authority of a man at Chiang's elbow; despairing at the Nationalist collapse, he took his own life in 1948.
